paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving scene from a single-camera video requires recovering both its three-dimensional shape and how that shape changes over time. 4RC addresses these together in one feed-forward framework. Its representation captures dense geometry and motion, extending beyond outputs such as a sparse collection of tracked points or motion between only two views.

The central design is to encode the video once and then query the resulting representation repeatedly. A transformer compresses the entire video into a compact representation of space and time. A conditional decoder uses this representation to return geometry and motion for a chosen query frame at a target timestamp. This separates the initial video encoding from subsequent requests for particular reconstruction outputs.

For learning, the method expresses each view’s changing scene through base geometry and relative motion that depends on time. This keeps geometry and motion jointly represented while giving them distinct roles. Experiments report improvements over prior methods across multiple reconstruction tasks, supporting the usefulness of a shared representation for recovering several aspects of dynamic scenes.
icml-2026-4rc-4d-reconstruction-via-cond.tldr: 4RC encodes a single-camera video once into a joint geometry-and-motion representation that supports reconstruction queries across frames and time.

paragraphs: Predicting the outcome of fine-tuning before paying for a complete run could save substantial computation. This paper examines the theoretical limits of that prediction problem. It treats the outcome as a stochastic quantity estimated from restricted information, making uncertainty itself an object of analysis rather than treating every prediction error as a weakness of the predictor.

The framework separates prediction risk into an intrinsic component associated with static data–model compatibility and a reducible component arising from optimization variability. The authors prove a lower-bound result that constrains how quickly optimization uncertainty can disappear, regardless of the predictor used. Within their formulation, improving the prediction algorithm alone therefore cannot make this uncertainty vanish arbitrarily quickly.

The analysis leads to a principle for allocating a probing budget and a diagram distinguishing Static-Sufficient, Dynamic-Critical, and Noise-Dominant regimes. These regimes organize when static information suffices, when observing training dynamics matters, and when noise dominates. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks support the predicted distinctions and the efficiency of the probing strategy, connecting theoretical uncertainty limits to practical decisions about preliminary training.
icml-2026-a-risk-decomposition-framework.tldr: The paper decomposes fine-tuning prediction risk to identify uncertainty limits and guide how much computation to spend on preliminary probes.

paragraphs: Adapting Segment Anything Model 2 to specialized tasks requires deciding both what to learn and how much adaptation capacity to provide. Fixed adapter structures can restrict that flexibility when downstream tasks vary in complexity. ACO-MoE-LoRA lets the adaptation structure evolve during training, combining ant colony optimization with a mixture of experts operating in latent space.

Its central module, ACO-ConvLoRA, uses a pheromone-guided mechanism to select experts and change their connectivity. Expert assignment becomes an evolutionary pathfinding problem. The method also adjusts LoRA ranks through weight slicing, allowing adapter capacity to change alongside parameter learning. Together, these mechanisms connect discrete choices about model structure with continuous optimization of model weights.

The authors report that this design mitigates routing collapse and addresses local-optimum problems associated with recent dynamic heuristics. Across 16 datasets, it consistently outperforms leading static adapters. The findings support adapting the organization and capacity of specialized components during training, rather than assuming that one fixed adapter arrangement will suit every task equally well.
icml-2026-aco-moe-lora-evolving-while-tr.tldr: ACO-MoE-LoRA evolves expert routing and adapter capacity during training to improve SAM2 adaptation across specialized domains.

paragraphs: Causal matrix completion estimates missing outcomes when the pattern of missing observations can depend on the data itself. Synthetic Nearest Neighbors addresses this setting by exploiting local low-rank structure through fully observed anchor submatrices. Its effectiveness, however, depends on having enough observations within each treatment level, which becomes difficult when treatments are numerous or complex.

Mixed Synthetic Nearest Neighbors extends this approach by integrating information across treatment levels when estimating an individual missing entry. The motivation is that a sparsely observed treatment need not be analyzed solely with the limited evidence available inside that treatment. Combining information enlarges the effective sample available to the estimator and directly addresses the data-availability bottleneck identified for the original method.

The authors show that the new estimator retains SNN’s finite-sample error bounds and asymptotic normality guarantees. These results preserve both error-control and distributional foundations while expanding the information used for estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness, particularly for treatment levels with scarce data. The contribution is therefore especially relevant to unevenly observed treatment settings.
icml-2026-causal-matrix-completion-under.tldr: MSNN pools information across treatment levels to improve causal matrix completion when individual treatments have few observations.

paragraphs: CentaurEval asks how much human involvement adds to coding agents. Traditional human tests and standalone AI benchmarks miss tasks where a person’s reasoning and an AI system’s implementation efficiency must work together. The benchmark therefore centers on problem templates designed to make collaboration necessary, placing joint problem-solving at the center of evaluation.

Tasks are generated dynamically from 45 templates. Human participants use a standardized development environment, while a reproducible toolkit provides 450 tasks for evaluating language models. The study compares 45 participants and five models across four levels of human intervention. This setup allows the authors to examine how different amounts of participation affect results on a shared family of coding problems.

Reported pass rates are 0.67% for models alone, 18.89% for humans alone, and 31.11% for collaboration. These results show a substantial benefit from working together on the benchmark’s deliberately demanding tasks. The analysis also finds that strategic breakthroughs can originate from either partner, supporting a view of collaborative coding in which both humans and AI contribute reasoning as well as execution.
icml-2026-centaureval-benchmarking-human.tldr: CentaurEval measures human–AI coding collaboration and finds higher success together, with strategic contributions coming from both partners.

paragraphs: Repository agents need to connect what software is intended to do with how its implementation is organized. Isolated documentation and dependency graphs provide only parts of that picture. RPG-Encoder treats understanding and generation as complementary operations: understanding compresses code into intent, while generation expands intent into code. It builds a shared representation to support that cycle.

The framework encodes raw code into a Repository Planning Graph that combines semantic features with dependency information. It updates the graph’s topology incrementally as the repository changes and provides a common interface for navigating code with awareness of its structure. The authors report a 95.7% reduction in maintenance overhead, addressing the cost of keeping this richer representation current.

Evaluations report 93.7% Acc@5 on SWE-bench Verified and an improvement exceeding 10% over the best baseline on SWE-bench Live, supporting stronger localization within complex repositories. On RepoCraft, reconstruction coverage reaches 98.5%. Together, these findings indicate that the graph can support both locating relevant implementation details and retaining enough information to reconstruct much of the original codebase.
icml-2026-closing-the-loop-universal-rep.tldr: RPG-Encoder combines code meaning and dependencies in an incrementally maintained graph that supports repository navigation and reconstruction.

paragraphs: CRAFT aims to make reasoning models more robust to jailbreak attacks by training the internal representations associated with their reasoning. Its objectives operate in hidden-state space as well as addressing safety-aware reasoning traces. The motivation is to align the reasoning process that leads to a response, extending safety training beyond the final text a model produces.

The framework combines contrastive representation learning with reinforcement learning. It separates representations of safe and unsafe reasoning trajectories, shaping the model’s internal geometry around that distinction. The theoretical analysis shows that adding consistency between latent representations and text to GRPO rules out superficially aligned policies as local optima. This is a statement about the optimization formulation, rather than an unconditional guarantee against every attack.

Experiments evaluate Qwen3-4B-Thinking and R1-Distill-Llama-8B across multiple safety benchmarks. CRAFT consistently outperforms defenses including IPO and SafeKey. Relative to the base models, the authors report average improvements of 79.0% in reasoning safety and 87.7% in final-response safety. The results support hidden-representation alignment as a useful way to improve both intermediate reasoning and visible responses.
icml-2026-contrastive-reasoning-alignmen.tldr: CRAFT combines contrastive learning and reinforcement learning in hidden-state space to improve reasoning-model safety against jailbreaks.

paragraphs: A robot can begin with a generative control policy trained on previously collected experience and then improve through its own interactions. DF-ExpEnse focuses on choosing those new interactions more effectively. Its goal is to make online fine-tuning more sample-efficient by improving the experience the robot collects, rather than treating action selection as a fixed part of adaptation.

The method uses the pretrained policy’s ability to represent multiple possible behaviors to construct an expressive candidate set that remains practical to evaluate. An ensemble of critics then selects the action that best balances expected quality with exploration interest. This combines the policy’s existing behavioral knowledge with a separate assessment of which available action is useful for learning.

For robot fleets, DF-ExpEnse additionally allows communication across agents to support coordinated exploration. The technique can be integrated with existing reinforcement-learning strategies for fine-tuning generative control policies. Across manipulation and locomotion tasks, experiments show consistent sample-efficiency improvements over default fine-tuning and alternative action-selection schemes. The findings suggest that better collection decisions can make self-generated experience more valuable during adaptation.
icml-2026-df-expense-diffusion-filtered-.tldr: DF-ExpEnse selects exploratory actions from pretrained generative policies to make online robotic fine-tuning more sample-efficient.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate multiple text positions in parallel, but deciding which positions to process together affects both speed and quality. Block-based inference helps avoid ordering problems associated with unrestricted bidirectional decoding. A fixed block schedule, however, treats semantically difficult and easy positions alike, sometimes committing uncertain text too early while making easier positions wait at block boundaries.

Dynamic Sliding Block changes this scheduling decision without retraining the model. It uses a sliding block whose size can vary, allowing the decoding schedule to adapt to semantic difficulty. The contribution concerns how inference is organized: the scheduler gains flexibility to process positions according to their difficulty instead of following a rigid partition established in advance.

The authors also introduce DSB Cache, a training-free key–value caching mechanism designed for the dynamic schedule. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks find that DSB together with its cache consistently improves generation quality and inference efficiency. These results support scheduling as a practical source of improvement, showing that the organization of parallel decoding can matter alongside the underlying model’s capabilities.
icml-2026-dsb-dynamic-sliding-block-sche.tldr: DSB adapts decoding blocks to semantic difficulty and adds compatible caching to improve diffusion language models without retraining.

paragraphs: Deep research agents can spend substantial time gathering evidence and writing reports, making an ambiguous initial request expensive to misunderstand. IntentRL trains an agent to clarify the user’s underlying intent before starting that extended work. The aim is to improve the direction of research early, when interaction can still shape what the system investigates and produces.

Because suitable open-ended research dialogues are scarce, the framework expands a small set of seed examples through a graph that progressively refines intent from shallow to deeper descriptions. Training then proceeds in two reinforcement-learning stages. The first uses offline dialogues to learn general interaction behavior efficiently. The second generates online interactions between the trained agent and a simulated user to improve adaptation to varied feedback.

Experiments report significant improvements in both intent hit rate and downstream task performance. IntentRL outperforms built-in clarification modules from closed-source research agents and proactive language-model baselines. The findings connect clarification quality with the usefulness of subsequent research, supporting explicit training for intent discovery as part of an autonomous research workflow.
icml-2026-intentrl-training-proactive-us.tldr: IntentRL trains research agents to clarify user intent before lengthy research, improving intent identification and downstream results.

paragraphs: MICE-Bench evaluates image creation and editing when a model must combine information from several visual references. Existing evaluations often emphasize a single reference or a narrow task, leaving complex combinations underexamined. This benchmark makes the interaction among concepts central, testing whether models can preserve multiple requested properties while producing a coherent image.

The benchmark contains 3,119 test cases organized within one concept space. Its design spans seven visual dimensions and increases constraint density from two concepts to seven. Both data construction and evaluation are concept-centered, allowing analysis of how different requirements interact. The authors assess 13 models using an eight-dimensional evaluation metric, examining performance beyond a single overall measure of image quality.

Closed-source models have a clear advantage in the reported evaluations. Nevertheless, every evaluated model loses concept consistency and physical realism as conceptual complexity increases. The authors interpret this pattern as evidence of superficial composition rather than genuine synthesis of multiple concepts. The benchmark therefore exposes a shared difficulty: satisfying increasingly many visual requirements together, even when individual outputs may otherwise look capable.
icml-2026-mice-bench-a-challenging-and-c.tldr: MICE-Bench finds that image models struggle to preserve concept consistency and physical realism as multi-reference requirements become more complex.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks solve differential equations by training against both the equation and its boundary requirements. These objectives can produce gradients that point against one another, making optimization unstable or trapping it in poor local solutions. The paper investigates this conflict through the shape of the loss landscape and the dynamics of the training process.

The proposed method, Constraint-Aligned loss with Manifold Lifting, reformulates all zeroth-order terms into aligned constraints. Zeroth-order terms involve the modeled quantities themselves rather than their derivatives. This reformulation is intended to mitigate conflicting optimization signals. A separate delay factor helps the optimizer move past high-curvature regions, addressing another source of difficulty identified in the training landscape.

The motivation comes partly from limits of existing approaches: adaptive weighting may leave the underlying ill-conditioning unresolved, while hard constraints can be restricted to simple geometries. Experiments show that CAML significantly improves numerical stability and efficiency on highly complex PINN problems. The results support changing the constraint formulation and optimization behavior together as a way to make these physics-based learning systems easier to train.
icml-2026-mitigating-gradient-pathology-.tldr: CAML reformulates constraints and introduces a delay factor to reduce gradient conflicts and improve training stability in physics-informed neural networks.

paragraphs: MotionMAR reconstructs human motion from sparse observations by following its temporal hierarchy. Broad movement trajectories provide a coarse structure, while faster changes supply fine detail. The framework first estimates the global motion and then progressively refines it, using this organization to guide reconstruction when the observed tracking data is incomplete.

A temporal multi-scale tokenizer encodes motion at several resolutions, separating semantic movement from minor jitters. The Motion Autoregressive Network predicts within this compressed representation, beginning with coarse indices that establish global structure and then producing finer indices for detail. A Scale-Aware Control module incorporates sparse tracking measurements so that the generated motion remains aligned with what was actually observed.

A final Motion Refinement Network smooths successive poses and removes artifacts introduced by quantization. Each component therefore addresses a different part of reconstruction: representation, prediction across scales, observation alignment, and final continuity. Experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy on AMASS. The findings support using temporal structure explicitly when reconstructing detailed motion from limited measurements, with coarse predictions providing the basis for subsequent refinement.
icml-2026-motionmar-multi-scale-auto-reg.tldr: MotionMAR reconstructs human motion from sparse tracking data by predicting broad trajectories first and progressively refining temporal detail.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to detect changes as multiple streams of events arrive over time. The event rates can vary, and observations can be temporally dependent. Such a setting appears in areas including earthquake monitoring, climate observation, and epidemic surveillance. The task is to recognize a change promptly while controlling how often the system raises a false alarm.

The method represents the streams’ Poisson intensity functions using low-rank matrices, producing an adaptive nonparametric detector. Its algorithm processes the series in a single pass. The computational cost of each new observation remains constant with respect to elapsed series length, so processing a later observation does not become more expensive simply because the monitoring history has grown.

The authors provide guarantees for overall false-alarm probability and characterize detection delay under temporal dependence. They also derive a Matrix Bernstein inequality for temporally dependent Poisson event series as part of the theoretical contribution. Numerical experiments demonstrate statistical robustness and computational efficiency. Together, the results address both reliable change detection and the practical need to keep ongoing monitoring computationally manageable.
icml-2026-online-change-point-detection-.tldr: The paper develops an online detector for changing multivariate event rates with false-alarm guarantees and constant processing cost per observation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve flow-matching models for text-to-image generation, but it must assign credit to decisions made throughout generation. The paper identifies inaccurate advantage attribution as a central problem with step-level Group Relative Policy Optimization. If the optimization signal poorly reflects how individual steps contribute to an outcome, post-training can be less effective.

Group Chunking Policy Optimization changes the unit receiving that signal. It groups consecutive timesteps into coherent chunks and performs policy optimization at the chunk level. The authors argue that this grouping can mitigate the negative effects of inaccurate attribution. The key methodological choice is therefore the temporal scale of the update: a connected sequence of generation steps becomes the unit of reinforcement learning.

Experiments show improved performance on standard text-to-image benchmarks and preference alignment, with up to 43% additional gains over GRPO. That figure is a reported maximum rather than a uniform improvement across every evaluation. The findings support chunk-level optimization as a promising way to post-train flow-matching generators by better matching the optimization unit to sequences of related generation decisions.
icml-2026-principled-rl-for-flow-matchin.tldr: GCPO groups consecutive generation steps into chunks to mitigate credit-assignment problems when reinforcement-learning fine-tunes flow-matching image models.

paragraphs: ProConMV addresses interpretability and verification in diabetic retinopathy diagnosis using multiple views. It combines lesion masks, clinical text, and multi-view data, responding to systems whose predictions rely on one source and whose reasoning is difficult to trace. The aim is to connect a diagnostic result to identifiable lesion concepts and the evidence supporting them.

The framework uses multimodal prompt analysis and interactions between visual and textual concepts to learn from these inputs. During reasoning, it incorporates lesion concepts into causal reasoning chains linked with clinical guidelines. It also includes doctor intervention as part of human–machine collaboration. These elements make the reasoning process an explicit part of the framework, alongside the final diagnostic decision.

For combining views, the authors derive a generalization-error upper-bound reduction from incorporating uncertainty about both lesion concepts and disease grading. This motivates a module that uses both uncertainties for fusion and provenance-based verification. Experiments on two public multi-view datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The theoretical result concerns an error bound, while the empirical findings support the framework’s diagnostic and interpretability approach.
icml-2026-proconmv-provenance-enabled-co.tldr: ProConMV combines multiple diagnostic views, lesion concepts, and uncertainty estimates to make diabetic retinopathy predictions more traceable and verifiable.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to acquire new tasks without losing what it learned earlier. Tasks can introduce overlapping or contradictory information, creating conflicts in their internal representations. SABER treats these conflicts as something to organize directly. Its motivation extends beyond isolating parameters or assigning separate modules to reduce interference between tasks.

The method first aligns representations within a unified subspace framework, providing a basis for shared task knowledge. It then decomposes task-specific information into orthogonal components to preserve distinct contributions. Finally, an energy-aware balancing mechanism recombines those components while maintaining stability. These stages jointly address what can be shared, what should remain distinguishable, and how the resulting information should contribute to the model.

Across multiple continual-learning benchmarks, SABER matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods. The reported results support structured management of representational conflict as an effective approach to retaining knowledge during sequential learning. The contribution is a coordinated way to align, separate, and rebalance task information, making the relationships among learned representations an explicit part of adaptation.
icml-2026-saber-continual-learning-with-.tldr: SABER manages conflicts between sequential tasks by aligning, separating, and balancing their representations to support learning without forgetting.

paragraphs: Discrete flow matching offers a way to generate graphs, but existing adaptations can become complicated and expensive to sample. Task-specific heuristics add tuning choices and can compromise the continuity equation underlying the approach. Some methods also need roughly as many sampling steps as diffusion models, reducing the practical benefit of using flow matching.

SimGFM simplifies the process by using characteristic patterns in graph-generation trajectories. Its design relies only on the scheduler and rate matrix, removing heavy heuristics and extensive hyperparameter tuning. These two elements govern the progression of generation and its transition rates. The central claim is that a simpler design can preserve strong generation performance while requiring substantially fewer steps.

On QM9, SimGFM matches prior models that need 500–1000 steps using only 10. Across most evaluated datasets, 50 steps match or surpass those baselines. The findings establish competitive empirical quality alongside large reductions in sampling steps. They also show that the additional machinery found in existing graph flow-matching adaptations is not required to obtain strong results in these evaluations.
icml-2026-simgfm-simplifying-discrete-fl.tldr: SimGFM simplifies discrete flow matching for graph generation while matching strong prior results with substantially fewer sampling steps.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents can gradually lose their ability to learn from new experience, a problem called plasticity loss. Mixture-of-experts networks can support diverse skills, yet their performance can still deteriorate during continual learning. This paper examines that deterioration through spectral plasticity, using Neural Tangent Kernel theory to formalize the loss of learning capacity in these policies.

The authors derive a tractable proxy for spectral plasticity using the feature matrices of individual experts. This provides a quantity that can guide a practical training intervention. SPHERE applies a Parseval penalty tailored to mixture-of-experts policies, with the goal of alleviating the spectral deterioration identified by the analysis. The theoretical framing thus leads to a specific regularization method.

On MetaWorld and HumanoidBench, SPHERE improves average success in continual reinforcement learning by 133% and 50%, respectively, compared with an unregularized mixture-of-experts baseline. It also maintains higher spectral plasticity throughout training. The paired findings connect the targeted property with better task performance in these evaluations and support regularization as a way to preserve adaptability over ongoing learning.
icml-2026-sphere-mitigating-the-loss-of-.tldr: SPHERE regularizes mixture-of-experts policies to preserve spectral plasticity and improve success during continual reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Creating a tabletop scene from a task description requires both understanding the requested arrangement and placing objects in physically plausible poses. Language-model layout predictions can produce collisions or floating objects because three-dimensional spatial reasoning is difficult. STABLE separates semantic planning and physical correction into complementary modules that work together to produce scenes ready for simulation.

A Semantic Reasoner, fine-tuned on structured tabletop scenes, generates a coarse layout from the task instructions. A Physics Corrector then uses a physics-aware flow-based denoising model to predict pose updates. These updates refine the arrangement while preserving its connection to the requested task. The system therefore explicitly couples the meaning of a scene with its physical validity.

Generation proceeds progressively, alternating the two modules as the scene grows from task-critical objects to background objects. This gives semantic planning and physical refinement recurring roles throughout construction. Experiments report simulation-ready scenes that strictly follow task instructions and substantially improve physical validity over prior approaches. The findings support combining language-based planning with learned physical correction for instruction-driven scene generation.
icml-2026-stable-simulation-ready-tablet.tldr: STABLE alternates semantic layout generation and physical correction to create instruction-aligned tabletop scenes ready for simulation.

paragraphs: Self-consistency improves language-model answers by generating multiple samples and combining their results. This can be computationally expensive, especially when entire answers are compared as indivisible units and sampling ends according to a fixed rule. TMAFC addresses both issues by changing how agreement is measured and how the system decides whether to generate another sample.

Fractal-Consistency examines individual components of outputs, allowing partially correct material from different samples to be combined. This makes useful agreement within answers available to the aggregation process. Adaptive Stopping Criteria Calibration then adjusts the stopping rule using real-time assessments of task difficulty and model capability. The framework can therefore vary its sampling effort with both the problem and the model attempting it.

Experiments across diverse question-answering benchmarks show a better balance between sampling cost and accuracy. The authors report sample-cost reductions of up to 55% while retaining competitive accuracy against state-of-the-art baselines. The result supports extracting more value from each sampled answer and calibrating when to stop, without claiming that every task receives the maximum reported saving.
icml-2026-task-and-model-aware-fractal-c.tldr: TMAFC combines agreement among answer components with adaptive stopping to reduce reasoning sample costs while maintaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning can consume substantial computation and sometimes make a model worse, depending on the data and training choices. TuneAhead predicts performance before committing to a complete run. It uses a short standardized training probe, so the prediction is available before full training rather than requiring no training activity at all.

Each proposed run becomes a feature vector combining static descriptions of its dataset with dynamic measurements from the probe. A predictor converts these features into an estimated performance score. SHAP-based attributions explain which features drive that estimate, providing diagnostics alongside the prediction. This makes the output useful both for screening a run and for understanding the predictor’s assessment.

Across more than 1,300 fine-tuning runs on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, TuneAhead consistently outperforms Early-Stop Extrapolation and ProxyLM. On 370 held-out runs, its root mean squared error is 1.47 percentage points, and 95.1% of predictions fall within three percentage points of the actual score. These results support screening policies that can avoid unnecessary full runs while retaining most promising candidates within the evaluated setting.
icml-2026-tuneahead-predicting-fine-tuni.tldr: TuneAhead combines dataset features and a short training probe to predict fine-tuning performance and screen candidate runs before full training.

paragraphs: UltraHorizon evaluates agents on extended discovery tasks where the environment is only partially observable. Agents must uncover hidden rules through repeated interaction while sustaining reasoning, planning, memory management, and tool use. Exploration provides a shared task structure across three environments, allowing the benchmark to examine capabilities that short, fully observable evaluations may leave under-tested.

The tasks require substantial sustained activity. Standard configurations average more than 35,000 tokens and 60 tool calls, while the heaviest setting averages more than 200,000 tokens and 400 calls. These lengths make continued management of information and actions central to performance, rather than evaluating only whether an agent can produce a useful response or complete a brief sequence.

Experiments find that agents using state-of-the-art language models consistently underperform human participants, and simple scaling fails to resolve the benchmark’s challenges. Analysis of their trajectories identifies eight error types, attributed to in-context locking and fundamental gaps in functional capabilities. The findings establish a gap in long-horizon exploration within these environments and provide a framework for examining where extended agent behavior breaks down.
icml-2026-ultrahorizon-benchmarking-agen.tldr: UltraHorizon exposes persistent weaknesses in agents’ sustained exploration, planning, and memory use across very long discovery tasks.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation replaces a large training set with a small synthetic one. This paper asks why different matching objectives can achieve that goal and how far a distilled set remains useful when training configurations change. Its configuration-dynamics-error framework measures the test-risk gap between models trained on distilled data and those trained on the full dataset.

The framework represents a training configuration as an update operator that determines optimization dynamics. Gradient, distribution, and trajectory matching are then understood as reducing the same dynamics-induced risk gap. Within a fixed configuration, the analysis predicts that the gap decreases at order k to the power of minus one-half as the distilled set size k grows, until reaching a configuration-dependent floor.

Across configurations, an order-tight coverage law says the required set size grows linearly with configuration diversity measured through covering-number complexity. This formalizes a boundary on how broadly a small distilled dataset can serve different training setups. Experiments with representative methods and configuration changes behave consistently with both laws, supporting guidance on when enlarging the synthetic set helps and when reducing the error floor matters more.
icml-2026-utility-boundary-of-dataset-di.tldr: The paper unifies dataset-distillation objectives and derives laws linking their usefulness to synthetic-set size and training-configuration diversity.

paragraphs: In highly stochastic environments, repeated observations can vary greatly even when the underlying decision problem stays the same. VarDE addresses pure exploration by asking where additional sampling will most reduce uncertainty in the final decision. This makes the reliability of the eventual choice the organizing principle for distributing sampling effort across components of a problem.

The method represents final-decision uncertainty through a smooth decision function. From that formulation, it derives allocation rules that account for how noise in individual components affects the final output. The relevant question is therefore how each source of variability propagates into the decision, giving a principled basis for deciding which observations deserve more sampling.

The authors apply the methodology to best-arm identification, Monte Carlo tree search, and best-policy identification. They provide theoretical guarantees concerning variance decay and simple regret, linking sampling allocation to both uncertainty reduction and decision quality. Experiments show consistent, significant improvements over existing methods, with especially strong gains in highly stochastic settings. The results support a common decision-focused approach across these three exploration problems.
icml-2026-variance-driven-exploration-a-.tldr: VarDE allocates exploration samples according to how much they reduce uncertainty in the final decision, improving performance especially under strong stochastic noise.
